papers.title: Coupling Raman Spectroscopy and Acoustic Microscopy to Characterize Glioblastoma Resistance
papers.abstract: Therapy resistance in glioblastoma is usually described in genetic or metabolic terms. Here we ask whether it also has a measurable biophysical form. Combining Raman spectroscopy with scanning acoustic microscopy on TRAIL-sensitive and TRAIL-resistant glioblastoma cells, we find that resistance carries both a biochemical and a mechanical signature: the resistant cells differ at protein, lipid and nucleic-acid bands, contain 4.1-fold more neutral lipid, and hold a high acoustic impedance that does not change when the drug is applied, while sensitive cells stiffen as they die. Because acoustic impedance is an absolute quantity and neither measurement requires a label, the approach offers a route to recognising resistant populations from their physical state alone.

papers.title: Freshwater Blackworms Solving a Maze
papers.abstract: We investigated the behaviour of freshwater blackworms (emph{Lumbriculus variegatus}) in a circular maze containing food in its central chamber. Analysis of 11 time-lapse recordings showed that all tested worms entered the central chamber, although first-arrival times and spatial exploration patterns varied substantially. Registered occupancy maps revealed non-uniform use of corridors and chambers. Because the study did not include a no-food control, the observations demonstrate central-chamber entry and spatial exploration but do not by themselves establish food localisation or chemotaxis. The assay provides a reproducible framework for studying annelid exploration and for future controlled comparisons of sensory cues and maze complexity.

papers.title: High-throughput affinity profiling of antibodies against soluble and native membrane targets by digital flow cytometry
papers.abstract: Binding affinity measurements are essential for optimizing and validating therapeutic and research antibodies, yet no high-throughput platform supports quantitative affinity measurements for both soluble and native membrane targets. Here we present a suite of digital flow cytometry (dFC) assays that determine equilibrium binding affinities by directly counting free and bound molecules in homogeneous mixtures without immobilization. The assays enable titration-free absolute KD measurements for fluorescent binding partners, affinity measurements for unlabeled antibodies against membrane receptors on cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), and multiplexed assays for rapid ranking or screening of antibody variants. We demonstrate applications by quantifying the effects of degree-of-labeling on the affinity of antibody-dye conjugates, and of drug conjugation on therapeutic antibody binding to receptors on human cancer EVs. By combining single-molecule quantitation, adaptable assay designs, and high-throughput analysis, dFC provides a versatile platform for therapeutic antibody optimization and research antibody validation.

papers.title: From coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to continuum models of biomolecular condensation
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensation contributes to cellular organization and the regulation of numerous biochemical processes. Capturing its dynamics on large spatio-temporal scales requires a macroscopic model that accurately describes both thermodynamic forces and molecular transport. Here, we investigate the applicability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation for modeling phase-separation dynamics in intrinsically disordered proteins. Using the low-complexity domain of FUS as a model system for biomolecular condensation, we perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to infer the free-energy functional and mobility coefficient entering the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The resulting continuum model accurately describes the growth of initial concentration fluctuations in the spinodal regime and the subsequent morphological evolution of the concentration fields during coarsening. We find that the free-energy functional is transferable across different stages of phase separation, whereas the mobility is not. During coarsening, we identify two kinetic regimes characterized by distinct mobilities, which persist even when a concentration-dependent mobility is introduced.

papers.title: Localization accuracy in single-molecule fluorescence microscopy
papers.abstract: The two prevalent methods to determine the position of individual fluorophores in the focal plane of a microscope rely either on the centroid of the fluorescence pattern produced by the fluorophore on a camera or on targeting the fluorophore's coordinate with a spatially controlled illumination minimum, as realized in MINFLUX. In both methods, (sub)nanometer localization precisions have been reached, but little is known about their accuracy, i.e., the deviation of the obtained coordinate from its ground truth. Here we report a theoretical and experimental comparison of the accuracy provided by these two strategies. We quantify substantial systematic errors in camera-based localization due to the interplay of two difficult-to-control parameters: the orientation of the fluorophore in space and its axial deviation from the focal plane (defocus). For example, within an axial range of {+/-}120 nm around the focus, the median distance between two fluorophores on a nanobody measured by camera-based localization varies by 26.5 nm. Under the same conditions, a commercial MINFLUX system yields a median variation in distance of 1.4 nm, indicating an improvement in accuracy by an order of magnitude. The accuracy of MINFLUX localization can be further improved to (sub-)[a]ngstrom levels by reducing the average distance between the coordinates targeted by the illumination minimum and the fluorophore. As it delivers unrivaled precision and accuracy for mapping fluorophores and their distances, we consider coordinate-targeted localization essential for studying labeled cells at the sub-10 nm level and for exploring structural and conformational changes of labeled biomolecules.

papers.title: Temperature-responsive contacts in TRPV1 concentrate in the cytoplasmic coupling domains
papers.abstract: TRPV1, the heat-activated cation channel of pain-sensing neurons, is a major target for new analgesics, yet where it senses heat remains unresolved. Candidate sensors have been proposed in nearly every part of its structure, from the ankyrin repeats to the pore. Here we ask where the contact network of the closed channel responds to temperature. We simulated human TRPV1 in a multicomponent membrane at six temperatures spanning its activation threshold and three salt concentrations, at atomistic and coarse-grained resolution. We decomposed the contacts that recur across its four identical subunits into collective thermal modes and tested each mode against temperature and, as a control, salinity. Only the leading atomistic mode follows temperature, which explains 59% of its variance and no mode follows salinity at either resolution. The temperature mode places 80% of its variance in the cytoplasmic domains, against 63% of all contact variance, and is most enriched in the linker domain that joins the ankyrin repeats to the transmembrane domain. On heating, the linker releases the C-terminal domain and binds the ankyrin repeats more tightly. Lipid contacts cluster along the transmembrane and TRP domains, and the few that reach the ankyrin repeats and the linker are mostly with the anionic inner-leaflet phosphatidylserine. The coarse-grained model reproduces the atomistic fluctuations and lipid organization, but the temperature mode emerges only at atomistic resolution. Its localization matches that of the dominant temperature mode of the related channel TRPV3. These results narrow the search for the heat sensor. In both channels, the contact network responds to temperature not in the pore but in the cytoplasmic coupling region where the ankyrin repeats, the linker, and the C-terminal domain meet.

papers.title: The Signaling Pathway of a Bacterial Two-Component System Determined by cryo-EM
papers.abstract: Although two-component systems (TCSs) play ubiquitous roles in sensing signals for bacterial survival and virulence, a detailed structural map of the signal transduction pathway is lacking. Bacteriophytochromes (BphPs) are enzymatic photoreceptors with homologs in plants that regulate bacterial physiological responses via TCS signaling. Here, we employ cryo-EM to elucidate the structural basis of a light-regulated TCS by capturing the full-length BphP histidine kinase (HK) in complex with its downstream response regulator (RR). The RR binds as a dimer to the HK but contacts the enzyme only through one subunit. Light absorption perturbs the entire BphP structure, including the HK domain, which disrupts phosphorylation and phosphotransfer reactions and promote TCS complex dissociation. Thus, light controls signaling through both HK activity and reversible binding of the RR.

papers.title: Mechanical characterization of human centromeres
papers.abstract: Centromeres must withstand high pulling forces in metaphase, yet allow rapid and complete chromosome segregation in anaphase. Using optical tweezers measurements on isolated human metaphase chromosomes, we find that centromeres are stiffer at low forces and more frequently exhibit pronounced softening compared to whole chromosomes, while displaying a similar stiffening response at high forces. We capture these mechanical properties by establishing a softened hierarchical worm-like chain model. Cohesin cleavage alters the mechanical properties of centromeres but does not lead to chromosome segregation in vitro. Topoisomerase II is recruited to centromeric regions under significant tension, likely to resolve the persistent centromeric DNA entanglements that provide additional sister chromatid cohesion. These findings advance our understanding of the mechanical resilience and regulation of centromeres during mitosis.

papers.title: Dual role of the RIG-I 2CARD as a signaling module and a brake on dsRNA translocation
papers.abstract: RIG-I is an innate immune receptor for viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Upon binding dsRNA, RIG-I nucleates MAVS filaments through its two caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD). However, how the 2CARD behaves during activation has remained unclear. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy, we visualized the 2CARD in full-length RIG-I across its apo, dsRNA-bound, translocating, multimeric, and polyubiquitin-bound states. Protrusions consistent with the 2CARD appeared only transiently in the apo state, whereas a mobile 2CARD emerged upon RNA binding. During ATP-driven translocation, wild-type RIG-I moved approximately twofold slower and showed more frequent pauses and multimers than RIG-I {Delta}2CARD. Within multimers, 2CARDs formed a complex that polyubiquitin stabilized into larger, dsRNA-deforming assemblies. These findings reveal the 2CARD as a brake on the RIG-I motor, beyond signaling.

papers.title: Understanding the role of chromatin accessibility and compaction on loop extrusion dynamics
papers.abstract: Loop extrusion by SMC complexes is a fundamental mechanism regulating the three-dimensional genome organization, but how these molecular motors navigate through the crowded, nucleosome-covered chromatin fiber remains an open question. Here, we develop a stochastic biophysical model of loop extrusion that explicitly couples motor stepping dynamics to chromatin accessibility and compaction. First, we systematically analyze the role of accessibility on its dynamics across homogeneous, periodic, and random roadblock positioning along chromatin. This comprehensive analysis reveals distinct dynamic regimes: phase-dependent kinetics in periodic arrays where motor step size aligns with obstacle spacing, and anomalous sub-linear progression in disordered environments due to rare but long-lived trapping events. Then, we contextualize our framework to nucleosome-like arrays. Our simulations reveal a non-intuitive dual role for nucleosomes: while they hinder extruder progression by blocking access to linker DNA, their high compaction packs more base pairs per physical distance, enabling larger genomic displacements per step. Strikingly, the resulting base-pair extrusion speed displays a non-monotonic dependence on nucleosome spacing, reaching a maximum at intermediate linker lengths (10-70 bp) that can exceed the speed on naked DNA. Finally, in support of this mechanism, analysis of yeast genomic data shows that a higher nucleosome occupancy between cohesin-associated regions correlates with stronger contact enrichment, consistent with compaction-enhanced extrusion efficiency in vivo. These findings establish chromatin architecture as a tunable regulator of loop extrusion, explaining the comparable speeds observed in vitro and in vivo and providing a quantitative framework for understanding how genome organization emerges from the interplay between motor kinetics and chromatin structure.

papers.title: DiffuChannel: A Conditional Denoising Diffusion Model that Synthesises Single-Molecule Patch-Clamp Data with Exactly Known Idealisation (Ground Truth)
papers.abstract: Development of computational models for single-channel patch-clamp analysis is hampered by limited availability of labelled (idealised) data. Since experiment alone cannot provide a genuine ground truth, two simulation methods are commonly employed; Stochastic sampling from a specified Markov model, augmented with synthetic noise allows creation of unlimited, flawlessly idealised/annotated datasets, yet its authenticity hinges entirely on the premises underlying data and noise generation. A more recent method uses GAN-based generation, this also replicates real-world noise and artefacts, but does not include a ground truth idealisation or annotation and training is notoriously unstable. Here, we introduce DiffuChannel, a conditional noise-removal diffusion model that addresses these drawbacks. Channel dynamics come directly from a user-defined discrete-time Markov chain (or a model fitted to biological seed data), thus, the state assignment for each synthetic trace is precisely determined by design. The diffusion model is then trained exclusively to capture the noise distribution of raw current conditioned on a given idealisation, thereby replicating genuine noise, filtering, and artefact patterns observed in real data without needing to hand craft noise models. We use a two-step coarse-to-fine workflow that starts with a defined slow-envelope component conditioned on longer-term dwell-time features extracted from the input idealisation. This allows a degree of baseline drift and time-dependent relaxations to be captured over timescales far longer than the network's field of view. At generation time, we use a context-preserving inpainting method that enables creation of relatively seamless traces of any desired duration. We demonstrate that with only a limited set of labelled seed traces, synthetic records yield realistic all-points amplitude distribution, noise power spectrum, autocorrelation pattern, and slow envelope comparable to the source data. The model achieves a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between windowed real and generated data of 0.005 (median across the five phenotypes). This compares to a within real-split-half MMD value of 0.002 and an amplitude-matched white noise MMD value of 0.108. In this paper, we benchmark this against DeepGANnel. Since the underlying Markov model is defined rather than estimated, DiffuChannel generates infinite, perfectly labelled, phenotype-consistent training data ideal for developing and testing idealisation algorithms. We find that, in practice, this new method is far more stable than previous GAN models and runs start to end without human intervention. We provide the model open-source along with an interactive web-based training and synthesis interface/app.

papers.title: Microcalorimetry reveals bacterial motility as an expensive trait during starvation
papers.abstract: Quantifying the energetic costs of cellular traits is important to understand their evolutionary constraints and ecological function. However, direct measurements of energy expenditure of distinct traits are rare. Here, we present direct measurements of the power dissipation due to bacterial flagellar motility using microcalorimetry, based on measuring the power dissipation of a motile population and a non-motile mutant. For the single-flagellated marine bacterium textit{Vibrio coralliilyticus}, we determined the power dissipated by motility in cultures to be 0.91 W/mL/OD. Per swimming cell this amounts to 2.0E-15 W, or a turnover of 2.5E4 ATP molecules per second. The power dissipated for motility equals 35 % of total metabolism during starvation, indicating this is likely the most expensive cellular trait during starvation. The dissipation for motility is in good agreement with that predicted using resistive force theory, indicating that any thermodynamic inefficiencies upstream of the flagellar motor, such as metabolic inefficiencies, are small. We further show that the multiflagellated bacterium Escherichia coli dissipates 0.70 W/mL/OD when in motility buffer, comparable to marine bacteria despite the much lower swimming speed, and hence indicating lower efficiency of swimming. Finally, we show that the energy spent by Vibrio coralliilyticus on motility can have major consequences on their survival under starvation, causing a 40 % reduction in survival after 3 weeks of starvation of a motile compared to non-motile mutant. These results reveal the large costs involved in an individual trait that shapes microbial life in heterogeneous environments.

papers.title: AnDi-J: diffusion analysis of single-particle tracking data in Fiji
papers.abstract: Characterizing how particles diffuse is key to understanding biology across scales, yet extracting the underlying physical properties typically requires specialized tools rarely accessible to biology labs. Here we introduce AnDi-J, a Fiji plugin combining classical estimators with state-of-the-art machine learning for single-trajectory analysis and segmentation, requiring minimal knowledge of stochastic processes. It extracts diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents, classifies trajectories into diffusion models, and segments heterogeneous trajectories into diffusive states, through powerful, easy-to-use visualization tools. See more at https://github.com/gorkamunoz/andi-j .

papers.title: Dehydration-Responsive Left-Handed G-Quadruplexes Expandthe Sequence Repertoire
papers.abstract: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are widely studied noncanonical nucleic-acid structures that carry important biological functions. Typically, G4s form from G-rich sequences containing at least four tracts of more than two consecutive guanines, yet a plethora of unconventional G4-forming sequences have been identified, including sequences that fold into G4s only under specific conditions. These G4 states remain poorly resolved. Here we identify dehydration-responsive left-handed G4s (drLHG4s), a class of left-handed G4 (LHG4) structures accessible under dehydrating conditions. Using d(GT)n repeats, we show that left-handed folding depends on repeat length, salt condition and solvent conditions. Systematic mutational analysis reveals a broader but register-constrained sequence space, while high-resolution crystal structures of d-GTGGTGTGTGGTG, a sequence that folded robustly under dehydrating conditions, establish a bulged LHG4 architecture and reveal a distinctive hydration sphere. We further show that selected peptides and a cationic zinc phthalocyanine derivative, ZnTEGQPyrPc, containing four triethylene glycol methyl ether tails can induce LHG4 states. Together, our findings reveal a dehydration-responsive G4 landscape and expand the experimentally accessible sequence space of LHG4 folding.

papers.title: A chemical perturbation scan on a K2P channel modulator pocket identifies affinity hotspots
papers.abstract: Ion permeation in the two-pore-domain K+ (K2P) channel TREK1 is gated largely at the selectivity filter (SF), by a C-type-like inactivation mechanism involving distortions of the SF structure; and by a carbonyl flip, which disrupts K+ coordination. Both are prevented by a small-molecule activator bound adjacent to the SF, in a site termed the modulator pocket; yet which pocket regions carry the binding signal, and whether they couple to gating, is unclear. We use 46 chemical substitutions on the activator ML335, evaluated by non-equilibrium alchemical free-energy calculations, as an affinity perturbation scan on the lower- and upper pocket. The response is strongly asymmetric: Lower-ring substitutions impair binding, which we trace to a {pi}-{pi} stacking network connecting the M3, P2, P1 helices, and the SF. Conversely, upper-ring substitutions are tolerated and reshape contacts with the Cap-P1 and SF2-M4 loops; and with the upper SF. The identified affinity hotspots overlap with residues independently implicated in TREK gating by external cues such as pH, temperature, pressure, and cytosolic-sensor transduction, suggesting that high-affinity pocket sites might also shape the gating landscape.

papers.title: An inspectable Grover algorithm-based amplitude-amplification workflow for k-mer discovery and motif scanning with genomic coordinate traceability
papers.abstract: Motif discovery and motif scanning remain core primitives in genomics, but both tasks face combinatorial growth as k-mer length increases and as mismatch-tolerant searches expand the candidate space. In this work, we present MotifQu, a Python package and command-line tool that maps two common motif-analysis workflows-(i) scanning a genome for a user-specified consensus motif and (ii) de novo discovery of recurrent k-mers above a user-defined count threshold-onto Grover-style amplitude amplification circuits executed reproducibly via Qiskit Aer statevector simulation. We evaluate MotifQu on the SARS-CoV-2 reference contig (29,903 bp) and S. cerevisiae S288C reference genome, where the classical census identifies strongly non-uniform motif frequencies dominated by A/T-rich 5-mers and returns explicit coordinate lists across the full genome span. We further execute the same logical 10-qubit search on IBM hardware showing that while end-to-end execution is feasible, transpilation-induced circuit depth and entangling-gate volume produce a diffuse measurement distribution whose probabilities remain close to the uniform 1/1024 scale, limiting observable amplitude concentration under current NISQ constraints. Finally, we demonstrate the full discovery workflow on the S. cerevisiae S288C reference genome (12,157,105 bp) to illustrate search results (ranked motifs, probability summaries, circuit diagrams, and position plots) and to highlight the regime where a large, marked set reduces the sharpness of Grover amplification.

papers.title: Interlaboratory benchmarking of differential scanning fluorimetry reveals sources of variability in protein thermal stability parameters
papers.abstract: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) is widely used to assess protein thermal stability and to compare protein variants, ligands, or formulations with limited sample consumption. Yet, the reproducibility of DSF derived parameters across laboratories, instruments and analysis workflows remains poorly defined. Here, we report a two phase interlaboratory benchmark using a shared VHH sample across 26 laboratories, 28 instruments and seven DSF instrument models. In Phase 1, participants applied their routine acquisition and analysis workflows, whereas in Phase 2, acquisition conditions were harmonised. Datasets were analysed locally and then centrally reprocessed with MoltenProt. Participant reported apparent melting temperatures (Tm) showed good within instrument repeatability but moderate inter instrument dispersion. Harmonisation of acquisition conditions did not substantially reduce this dispersion. Conversely, centralised reprocessing narrowed the distribution among retained datasets, indicating contributions from analysis workflows and data acceptance criteria in addition to instrument dependent factors. Comparison with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) further showed that apparent Tm depended strongly on the fluorescence readout. For this VHH, single wavelength fluorescence at 350 nm showed the closest agreement with the DSC transition temperature, whereas the 350/330 nm ratio and barycentric mean generally yielded higher values. Furthermore, DSF derived apparent unfolding enthalpies were more variable than apparent Tm. Together, these findings show that DSF can be highly repeatable within a defined instrument and workflow, but that quantitative comparability across instruments depends on instrument specific effects, the choice of fluorescence readout and analysis strategy. Improved comparability will require transparent reporting of acquisition and analysis conditions, explicit data quality criteria, and well characterised reference materials to monitor instrument dependent offsets.

papers.title: Branching Suppresses Self-Aggregation while Preserving Membrane Association in SET-M33: An Atomistic Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: Branched antimicrobial peptides offer a promising strategy for improving the stability and activity of membrane-active peptides, but how branching alters self-association and membrane binding remains unclear. We used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to compare tetra-branched SET-M33 with its linear branch sequence Q33 (KKIRVRLSA) in water and at an anionic bacterial-membrane model, to do this, systems containing equivalent numbers of Q33 sequence units were simulated. Q33 formed dimers and higher-order oligomers, particularly at the membrane interface and under hydration-tuned enhanced sampling. In contrast, SET-M33 remained more dispersed, as the branched scaffold and its high cationic charge limited peptide-peptide association while allowing multivalent membrane binding. Both architectures associated rapidly with the bilayer but remained predominantly surface-bound, without persistent pore formation or complete insertion. Q33 showed stronger membrane-induced helical stabilization, whereas SET-M33 retained a more heterogeneous conformational ensemble. Overall, branching primarily altered lateral peptide organization while preserving close membrane association, suppressing uncontrolled self-aggregation and providing an atomistic rationale for the distinct behavior of SET-M33 relative to Q33.

papers.title: Prospective discovery of LasB inhibitors by integrating generative design, free energy ranking, and experimental validation
papers.abstract: Identifying synthetically accessible, potent ligands from vast chemical space remains a major challenge in drug discovery, particularly because experimental synthesis and testing are costly and low throughput. Here, we present a fully open-source computational-experimental workflow that integrates fragment-based de novo molecular design with rigorous alchemical absolute binding free-energy calculations to enable physics-based prioritization before chemical synthesis. We apply this strategy by targeting the virulence-associated zinc metalloprotease LasB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. From ~40,000 diverse compounds generated through multi-objective optimization, a small subset was prioritized and experimentally evaluated, leading to the discovery of three previously unreported nanomolar inhibitors (IC50 22-53 nM) with excellent metabolic and plasma stability. This work demonstrates a general and scalable framework for coupling generative molecular design with quantitative binding affinity prediction, improving decision-making and reducing the cost, time, and risk associated with early-stage drug discovery.

papers.title: GENIE: a multi-agent system for closed-loop autonomous microscopy
papers.abstract: Microscopy is foundational to biology, enabling direct observation of otherwise inaccessible cellular structures and processes. Artificial intelligence has advanced microscopy through acquisition control, image analysis, and natural language instrument operation. No system has unified these steps into a complete experimental loop. We introduce an autonomous multi-agent system that turns plain language goals into measurements and statistically tested answers, gating and executing every action in deterministic code. This sets the groundwork for extending microscopy from biological observation to autonomous investigation.

papers.title: A learning-to-rank framework for large-scale identification of unknown proteins from cryo-EM and cryo-ET maps
papers.abstract: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) can yield density maps whose molecular identities are unknown. Predicted-structure databases enable proteome-scale searches, but distinguishing the correct candidates remains challenging, particularly for intermediate-resolution maps without clear side-chain features. We developed CryoAssign, an automated framework that combines large-scale structure matching with learning-to-rank prioritization. CryoAssign searches intact density maps without prior segmentation and integrates complementary measures of map-model agreement. On held-out benchmark maps, CryoAssign robustly prioritized the correct candidates. It also identified proteins or narrowed the set of candidates in previously unassigned cryo-EM maps and recovered multiple components from complex cryo-EM and cryo-ET maps. Controlled low-pass filtering showed generally robust recovery across a broad range of intermediate resolutions. CryoAssign provides a scalable approach for identifying proteins from cryo-EM and cryo-ET density maps.

papers.title: Structural heterogeneity of uncrosslinked FtsH-HflKC assemblies includes variable FtsH occupancy and a distinct wild-type FtsH architecture
papers.abstract: The AAA+ metalloprotease FtsH associates with HflK and HflC to form the megadalton FtsH-HflKC complex (FHC), which contributes to membrane-protein quality control in Escherichia coli. Recent structural studies have revealed asymmetric HflKC architectures and variable FtsH occupancy, contrasting with earlier crosslinked structures of a symmetric four-hexamer cage. Here, we analyzed wild-type, uncrosslinked FHC co-expressed from a single multicistronic plasmid and solubilized in lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) using single-particle cryo-EM, SEC-SAXS, and biochemical activity assays. Two-dimensional classification identified HflKC-containing particles associated with one or two FtsH hexamers, together with a distinct population of isolated FtsH particles. Focused reconstruction of the FtsH cytosolic domain reached 5.32 angstrom resolution and provided a structural view of wild-type, uncrosslinked FtsH without stabilizing substitutions or an added nucleotide analogue. The reconstruction retained the characteristic stacked arrangement of the AAA+ and protease rings but showed a more laterally splayed AAA+ ring compared with the stabilized reference, while the protease ring remained broadly similar in overall envelope. A 9.63 angstrom HflKC consensus reconstruction and 3D variability analysis (3DVA) in C1, further revealed substantial conformational variability spanning open-like and more constricted scaffold geometries. SEC-SAXS of a selected later-eluting LMNG-solubilized fraction yielded a compact anisotropic envelope with an estimated Dmax of ~110-115 angstrom, although this species could not be assigned to a defined intact FHC stoichiometry. Under the conditions tested, the FHC preparation also showed lower apparent ATPase and proteolytic activities than isolated FtsH. Together, these findings highlight the compositional and conformational heterogeneity of uncrosslinked FHC and reveal a more laterally splayed AAA+ arrangement in wild-type FtsH compared with the stabilized reference structure.

papers.title: Chemokine-induced cell swelling fluidises the plasma membrane to regulate CD8+ T cell migration
papers.abstract: T cell migration is primarily viewed as a cytoskeletal process. Here, we show that chemokine-stimulated CD8+ T cell migration is modulated by a volume-driven biophysical switch at the plasma membrane (PM). We found that chemokine-induced cell swelling creates an adhesion-dependent gradient of high PM fluidity at the leading edge. External chemical fluidisation of the PM using membrane modulators enhances migration similar to chemokine-induced fluidisation without the need of cell-swelling. Together, our findings identify PM fluidity as a tuneable biophysical gatekeeper that controls T cell migration, potentially providing a novel mechanical tool for optimising adoptive cell therapies in restrictive tissue microenvironments.

papers.title: Human Metalloenzymes Are Disproportionately Linked to Disease: The HEAM Structural Annotation Resource
papers.abstract: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and 1,171 non-catalytic metalloproteins. HEAM incorporates annotated metals into protein structures at their corresponding binding sites and classifies each site as catalytic or non-catalytic using the machine learning classifier MAHOMES II. HEAM more than quadruples the human site-level coverage of the largest prior metalloenzyme database. Using HEAM, we show that human metalloproteins are significantly enriched in KEGG disease pathways relative to the human proteome, and that metalloenzymes specifically are significantly enriched in ClinVar pathogenic variants -- a distinction obscured in prior, catalytically unresolved metalloprotein datasets. These pathogenic variants are concentrated in metabolic disorders, indicating that metabolic dysfunction is a substantial contributor to metalloenzyme-linked disease. By pairing 3D structural annotation with catalytic classification, HEAM provides both a foundation for structure-guided drug design against metal-binding sites and a resource for determining how catalytic and non-catalytic metal function contribute to human disease.

papers.title: Structural basis for phosphorylation-induced inactivation of the rice ammonium transporter AMT1;1
papers.abstract: Ammonium (NH4+) uptake and transport in plants are mediated by ammonium transporters (AMTs), which are tightly regulated by phosphorylation to prevent excess ammonium influx and toxic accumulation. However, the mechanism of phosphorylation-mediated inactivation is unique and remains unclear. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of the rice (Oryza sativa) ammonium transporter OsAMT1;1 in its wild-type and phosphomimetic variant T452D states. OsAMT1;1 forms a stable homotrimer, with conserved motifs affirming a shared transport mechanism within the AMT/MEP/Rh superfamily. Our structural analysis reveals that T452D phosphomimetic stabilizes an intracellular salt-bridge network and maintains the channel in a closed state, in which the ICL5 loop positions the hydrophobic plug residue Leu360 near the cytoplasmic exit to occlude the channel exit and abolish complementation capacity. Our findings elucidate phosphorylation-induced inactivation mechanism for the plant AMT1 subfamily, providing a structural paradigm for the post-translational regulation of nutrient uptake.

papers.title: Functional dynamics of the eukaryotic RNA exosome upon complex formation
papers.abstract: Rather than being static, proteins adopt multiple conformations and undergo dynamics on a wide range of timescales. Such conformational changes can be routinely probed by solution state NMR for protein sizes below 40 kDa and can be extended to large protein complexes with selective methyl-labeling strategies. Here, we expand the limit of methyl-NMR dynamics experiments to asymmetric protein complexes bigger than 300 kDa by investigating the inert core of the eukaryotic RNA exosome, Exo9. We demonstrate that isolated subunits are highly dynamic on the ms-s dynamics, which facilitates assembly. While ring subunits lose dynamics upon complex-formation, cap subunits and functional loops retain a large degree of flexibility as demonstrated by relaxation dispersion and chemical exchange saturation transfer experiments in the fully asymmetric Exo9 complex. Employing EPR spectroscopy we additionally revealed changes in the conformational ensemble and nanosecond dynamics of a spin-labeled functional loop region in the presence of the catalytic subunit Rrp44 and in response to substrate RNA binding. We thus demonstrate that an integrated NMR-EPR approach facilitates the characterization of functional dynamics that occur on a wide range of timescales in very large protein complexes.

papers.title: PINPOINT enables non-destructive nanoscopic quality control of individual lipid nanoparticles and their mRNA cargo
papers.abstract: Quality control of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is central to development of mRNA therapeutics, yet ensemble measurements obscure critical heterogeneity in particle morphology and mRNA cargo loading. Here we introduce PINPOINT (Profiling Individual Nanoparticles with Precise Observation of INternalized Therapeutics), a single-particle nanoscopy platform for non-destructive, multiparametric profiling of preformulated LNP samples. Super-resolution imaging with Nile Red resolves size and morphology, while an optimized permeabilization strategy provides selective access to encapsulated mRNA without compromising LNP integrity. Single-particle fluorescence measurements, including RiboGreen and sequence-specific probes, enable quantification and validation of mRNA loading and identity. Comparative analyses of bare and encapsulated mRNA reveal kinetic and structural features, exposing heterogeneity masked by bulk assays. By integrating structural and molecular readouts at the single-particle level, PINPOINT establishes a quantitative framework for assessing of LNP composition and payload distribution, offering actionable insights for improving batch consistency and guiding the rational design of next-generation mRNA delivery systems.

papers.title: Lipid diffusion enhanced by molecular motors
papers.abstract: An experimental study of myosin I motors on a supported lipid membrane with a nematic actin filament layer is presented. The activities of myosin I motors re-organize the actin layer, in particular the morphology of +1/2 nematic defects. Data from single-particle tracking (SPT) of lipid molecules reveal two interesting features. First, the distribution of average lipid speed over a track shows two groups of lipids (high-speed and low-speed), and the proportion of lipids to be high-speed is higher in regions rich in actin. Second, by classifying short-time movement of the lipids into normal diffusion, directed motion, confined motion, and subdiffusion states, we found that lipids in regions rich in actin have a lower probability to stay in the confined and subdiffusion states and more likely to perform normal diffusion. Furthermore, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) measurements show that the diffusion of lipids in the actin-rich regions is enhanced. The SPT and FRAP results suggest that myosin I motor activities turn low-speed lipids to high-speed ones, and affect the lipid moving state by reducing confined and subdiffusive motion. As a result, lipid diffusion is enhanced by motor activities.

papers.title: Structural Basis for the Rational Design of UAMC-1110-Based FAP Radiopharmaceuticals
papers.abstract: Radioligands targeting fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) are promising tools for cancer diagnosis and therapy. However, the molecular binding mode of clinically established UAMC-1110-derived ligands such as FAPI-46 remains insufficiently characterized. To simplify synthesis while preserving key binding properties, we designed two novel derivatives - FAP-DD-101 (short aminoalkyl linker) and FAP-DD-102 (extended aminohexanoic acid spacer) - and evaluated them alongside FAPI-46 using molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Across all derivatives, we identified a highly stable, energetically favorable charge-anchored binding mode, in which the 2-cyano-4,4-difluoropyrrolidine head anchors in a negatively charged subregion formed by Glu202, Glu203, and Glu204, mimicking the binding architecture observed in the FAP-linagliptin complex. MD trajectories confirmed that FAPI-46 and FAP-DD-101 maintain exceptional stability in this pose, with several non-anchored FAPI-46 trajectories spontaneously evolving toward engagement with this electrostatic subregion. For FAP-DD-102, linker elongation slightly reduced pose robustness, yet initial charge-anchored states still yielded superior average binding energies and vector stability compared to non-anchored poses. Overall, these findings elucidate the key structural determinants of FAP recognition, establishing a rational framework for designing synthetically accessible FAPI radiotracers with retained binding stability.

papers.title: DNA nullomers as a statistical phenomenon
papers.abstract: Nullomers are sequences absent from a certain genome. Due to their unexpected occurrence in short sequences, a hypothesis is that they are avoided for evolutionary reasons or because they might have lethal consequences on organisms. However, we present evidence that the occurrence and frequency of nullomers in genomes is expected as a stochastic consequence of uneven base pair combination distributions in the genetic code. This is done by artificially constructing whole genomes from statistics with a Markov chain model. The number of nullomers in these artificial genomes is in good agreement with the nullomer counts in reference genomes. Additionally, we investigated the nullomers of over 200 human genomes and found large deviations in the nullomers between individuals, further supporting the hypothesis that a vast majority of nullomers is very unlikely to have lethal effects.
